planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing an extremely sturdy, large support such as a mature tree or big pergola, since Kiftsgate is one of the largest roses in cultivation.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing an exceptionally sturdy support such as a mature tree, since this selection of the wild Himalayan species Rosa filipes can climb 25 to 40 feet into a canopy and spread just as wide. In mid to late summer it produces enormous, airy, cascading sprays of small single white flowers with prominent golden stamens and a light musky fragrance, followed in autumn by masses of tiny orange-red hips that persist into winter and feed birds. Because it flowers only once a year and grows so immense, it belongs on a large property where it can scramble freely into an old tree or over an outbuilding rather than in a small tended border. Limit pruning to removing dead wood or controlling reach immediately after the summer bloom, since flowers form on the previous year's growth.

subcategory: species shrub rose grown for ornamental thorns

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in early spring once soil is workable, in an open site in full sun where low winter or morning light can backlight the young canes; this species rose is grown chiefly for its thorns rather than its flowers.

directions: Site this species rose where low sun, especially in winter and early morning, can shine through the young canes, since its huge, flattened, triangular thorns turn a translucent ruby-red and glow when backlit, making it one of the most striking rose species grown for structure rather than bloom. Small single white flowers with four petals (fewer than typical five-petaled roses) appear in late spring, followed by small pear-shaped orange-red hips, but the real show is the winged, blood-red thorns on new growth through winter. It grows into a large, open, arching shrub and is best sited as a specimen away from paths, since the thorns are exceptionally sharp. Prune out the oldest wood each winter to encourage fresh red-thorned canes, since the color is most vivid on young growth.

subcategory: species shrub rose grown for fragrant foliage

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in early spring in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun spot; this early-blooming Chinese species rose is grown as much for its aromatic foliage as its flowers.

directions: Brush or crush the small, fern-like, glossy leaflets of this Chinese species rose to release a strong incense-like scent that gives the plant its common name, most pronounced on warm, humid mornings. It is among the earliest roses to flower, opening single, cupped, primrose-yellow blooms that fade to white along upright, thorny, dark-brown stems in mid-spring, well before most other roses begin, followed by small rounded red hips. Give it a sheltered site in full sun with fertile, humus-rich soil, since its early flowers can be damaged by late spring frosts in exposed locations. It forms an open, arching shrub that needs only removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering, since like most once-blooming species roses it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: French Rose (Rose of Provins, Wild Gallica Species)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root suckering shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this is the wild European species from which the entire Gallica class of old garden roses descends.

directions: Plant the wild French Rose in average, even lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it tolerates poorer conditions and more neglect than almost any modern rose, in keeping with its status as one of the oldest roses in cultivation, grown in Europe since antiquity. It bears fragrant, deep pink to crimson, semi-double to double flowers in a single heavy flush in late spring, followed by small rounded hips, on a low, dense, suckering shrub that spreads over time to form a thicket. As the wild ancestor of the entire Gallica class, it is more compact and simpler-flowered than named Gallica cultivars but shares their toughness, disease resistance, and cold hardiness. Because it spreads by suckers, give it room to naturalize or plan to control its spread with a buried root barrier, and prune only to remove dead wood right after the spring bloom.

common_name: Königin von Dänemark Rose (Queen of Denmark, Fragrant Alba)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; introduced in 1826, this is one of the most fragrant and finely formed Alba roses.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil where the shrub receives at least a half day of sun, since Königin von Dänemark, like other Alba roses, tolerates lighter shade better than most garden roses while still flowering well. Introduced in Denmark in 1826, it produces intensely fragrant, fully double, quartered flowers that open deep pink and pale toward the outer petals, each centered with a distinct green button eye, in a single spectacular flush in early summer. Its blue-gray-green foliage and lax, arching canes benefit from light support to keep the heavy blooms from bowing to the ground, and the shrub is notably cold-hardy and disease-resistant even with minimal spray programs. Prune lightly only to remove dead or crossing wood right after the bloom flush, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Celestial Alba Rose (Céleste, Soft Pink Fragrant Alba)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Celestial (also sold as Céleste) is a Dutch Alba rose of unknown origin grown since the 1700s.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since Celestial, like other Alba roses, tolerates part shade better than most garden roses without sacrificing much bloom. Of unknown Dutch origin from the 1700s, it produces sweetly scented, semi-double, clear soft-pink flowers that open to reveal a few golden stamens, set against neat, gray-green foliage, in one heavy flush in early summer. It grows into a tall, robust, healthy shrub that is notably resistant to blackspot and mildew even with minimal care, making it a reliable choice for naturalistic or low-maintenance plantings. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since like other once-blooming Albas it sets buds on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Frau Karl Druschki Rose (White Hybrid Perpetual, Snow Queen Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bred in Germany and released in 1901, this Hybrid Perpetual is famed for its huge, pure white blooms.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, since Frau Karl Druschki, sometimes called the Snow Queen Rose or White American Beauty, needs good light and airflow to perform its best and resist blackspot. Bred by Peter Lambert and released in 1901, it produces very large, pure white, high-centered blooms with 25 to 40 petals on long stems, repeating in flushes from late spring through fall, though the flowers carry little to no fragrance. Its tall, somewhat narrow, upright growth habit makes it useful as a hedge or background shrub, and its stark white color reads well against darker foliage or brick. Deadhead spent blooms through the season to encourage continued rebloom, and prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain a strong framework.

common_name: Paul Neyron Rose (Giant Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bred in France and introduced in 1869, this Hybrid Perpetual is known for having some of the largest flowers of any rose.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, feeding generously through the growing season, since Paul Neyron rewards good care with some of the largest flowers of any rose, sometimes exceeding six inches across. Introduced in France in 1869, it bears fully double, warm pink blooms shaded with lilac, packed with 40 to 50 petals in an informal, cupped form, repeating in flushes from late spring into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its huge blooms are heavy enough to nod on the stem in wet weather, so a sheltered spot out of driving rain helps keep flowers looking their best. Deadhead through the season to encourage rebloom and prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain vigor and shape.

common_name: Ferdinand Pichard Rose (Striped Crimson-and-Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in France in 1921, this Hybrid Perpetual is prized for its candy-striped blooms and repeat flowering.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ferdinand Pichard is unusual among Hybrid Perpetuals for both its striking, candy-striped flowers and its reliable rebloom through the season rather than a single early flush. Introduced in 1921, it bears cupped, fully double, richly fragrant blooms in soft pink boldly striped with crimson and carmine, the pattern varying slightly from flower to flower, on a compact, well-branched shrub. Because it repeats its bloom more dependably than most old-fashioned striped roses, it rewards routine deadheading through summer and fall with continued flushes of color. Prune back by about a third in late winter and watch for blackspot in humid climates, giving the plant good air circulation to keep foliage healthy.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Jenny Duval is a Gallica of uncertain origin grown before 1842, valued for its shifting bloom color.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, though Jenny Duval appreciates a little afternoon shade in hot climates, since its petals can scorch and its colors fade faster in intense heat. Documented before 1842 and of uncertain origin, it bears loosely double, fragrant flowers that open warm mauve-pink and shift through the bloom period toward smoky grape and slate-violet, sometimes showing several color stages on the shrub at once. It grows as a vigorous, somewhat lax bush that flowers once in a heavy late-spring to early-summer flush, in keeping with its Gallica heritage, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably tough, disease-resistant, and cold-hardy, needing only removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Empress Josephine Rose (Veined Pink Antique Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Empress Josephine, sometimes classed as Rosa x francofurtana, is a historic rose predating 1815 known for its veined petals.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Empress Josephine tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as an antique rose predating 1815. It bears large, loosely double, cupped flowers in rich rose-pink with distinctive darker pink veining running through each wavy petal, giving the bloom a shot-silk effect unlike most other old garden roses. It flowers once in a full late-spring flush with a light, sweet fragrance, then rests for the remainder of the season, setting attractive rounded hips if not deadheaded. It is disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Petite de Hollande Rose (Compact Small-Flowered Centifolia)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact 18th-century Centifolia rose suits smaller gardens better than most old garden roses.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Petite de Hollande tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 18th-century Centifolia. It bears clusters of small, fully double, clear pink pompon-form flowers with a strong classic old-rose fragrance, produced in a single heavy flush in midsummer on a compact, bushy shrub notably smaller than most Centifolias. Its modest mature size makes it a good choice for gardeners who love the fragrance and form of old roses but lack room for a full-sized Cabbage Rose. Like other Centifolias it blooms once, then rests for the remainder of the season, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this miniature 18th-century Centifolia forms a small, dense bush suited to the front of a border.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rose de Meaux tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Centifolia. Known since the 1700s, it is a true miniature form of the Cabbage Rose, growing as a dense, twiggy, small-leaved bush covered in masses of tiny, fully double, clear pink pompon flowers with a light fragrance in a single midsummer flush. Its diminutive scale makes it useful at the front of a mixed border or in a large container, where its detail can be appreciated up close, unlike most old garden roses that need room to spread. Like other Centifolias it blooms once, then rests, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in spring once frost danger has passed, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-evergreen Chinese species rose forms a dense, sprawling, thorny mound and is marginally hardy outside the Deep South.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, giving this vigorous Chinese species rose plenty of room, since it forms a dense, sprawling, thorny mound or scrambling climber that can spread wider than it is tall. Introduced to the West in 1793, it bears large, single, pure white flowers with a prominent boss of golden stamens and a light fragrance from summer into fall, followed by small orange-red hips, against glossy, leathery, semi-evergreen foliage. It is markedly drought-tolerant once established and, in the Deep South where it is fully hardy, has naturalized along roadsides and fencerows, so give it a defined bed or an area where its spread is welcome. Its stiff, hooked thorns make it useful as an impenetrable barrier hedge, but prune with heavy gloves and cut back hard in late winter to control size.

common_name: Geranium Rose (Bright Red Moyesii Selection with Flask-Shaped Hips)
subcategory: species shrub rose grown for hips

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in early spring once the ground can be worked, giving this vigorous selection of Rosa moyesii ample room to develop its large arching mature size; raised at RHS Garden Wisley in 1938.

directions: Choose a permanent site in full sun with good drainage, since Geranium, a Rosa moyesii selection raised at RHS Garden Wisley in 1938 and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, grows into a large arching shrub that resents disturbance once established. It bears brighter, more vivid scarlet-red single flowers than the wild species, opening along the canes in early summer, followed by an outstanding fall display of large, flagon-shaped orange-red hips that persist into winter and outshine the earlier bloom. Water regularly the first year to establish deep roots, then reduce supplemental irrigation as the plant matures and becomes quite drought-tolerant. Site it as a specimen or back-of-border shrub where its size, arching form, and spectacular hip display have room to be appreciated, and limit pruning to removing dead wood.

common_name: Aimée Vibert Rose (Vigorous White Climbing Noisette)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy support; bred in France and introduced in 1828, Aimée Vibert is a nearly thornless climbing Noisette.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, wall, or trellis, since Aimée Vibert, introduced in France in 1828, is a vigorous, nearly thornless climbing Noisette that can reach 15 feet or more with support. It bears large, cascading clusters of small, fully double, pure white flowers with a fresh musky fragrance, repeating in flushes from summer through fall more reliably than many older Noisettes, set against glossy, disease-resistant foliage. Its near absence of thorns makes it easy to train and maintain along a doorway or arbor where visitors brush past it. Once established it tolerates drought and lean soil well, and needs only routine thinning of old wood in late winter to keep it productive and well-shaped.

common_name: Devoniensis Rose (Magnolia Rose, Antique Climbing Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a sturdy support; introduced in England in 1838 and popularized in its vigorous climbing form found in the American South, this Tea rose is called the Magnolia Rose for its huge creamy blooms.

directions: Plant own-root shrubs in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with excellent air circulation and a sturdy support, since the climbing form of Devoniensis, discovered as a sport in the American South, can scale 20 feet or more given a wall or pergola. Introduced in England in 1838, it is called the Magnolia Rose for its huge, creamy ivory blooms flushed with pink, yellow, or buff depending on weather, opening from plump buds with an intense, fruity Tea fragrance. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall where winters stay mild, but the thin petals can ball in prolonged humidity, so siting it where morning sun dries the foliage quickly improves bloom quality. It needs winter protection or a very sheltered site outside the Deep South and Gulf Coast, and benefits from light, frequent feeding and minimal hard pruning to keep its climbing canes productive.
sources: Antique Rose Emporium — Devoniensis variety notes

common_name: Catherine Mermet Rose (Fragrant Light Pink Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation; bred in France and introduced in 1869, this Tea rose was once a major cut-flower variety and prefers a warm, dry climate.

directions: Plant own-root shrubs in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with good air circulation; Catherine Mermet, introduced in France in 1869, was once grown by the acre as a florist's cut flower for its perfectly formed, light silvery-pink, fully double blooms with a classic Tea fragrance. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall on a graceful, moderately vigorous bush, performing best in a warm, dry climate, since its foliage is more susceptible to blackspot and mildew in humid regions than tougher Tea roses. Give it a sheltered site out of harsh wind and provide light, frequent feeding through the growing season to keep flushes coming. In marginal zones, mound soil or mulch over the graft or crown for winter protection, and prune only lightly, since Tea roses resent hard pruning.
